title: Bank Reconciliation Statement
outcomes: Read a pass book or bank statement and explain why its balance is the mirror image of the bank column of the cash book.
Identify every reason why the two balances differ — timing gaps, items the bank records first, and errors by either side.
Prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement starting from any of the four balances (favourable or overdraft, cash book or pass book), in both the "balance" and the "plus & minus" layouts.
Prepare an adjusted (amended) cash book first and then reconcile, and state which bank balance goes to the balance sheet.
Explain why regular reconciliation is a core internal control against errors and fraud.

meta.exam_tip: BRS is a regular 4–10 mark question. The marks go to correct add/less signs, correct treatment of an overdraft and a clean statement with a proper heading "as on <date>". Practise starting from all four balances.

concepts.title: Pass book versus the cash book's bank column
body: Every bank transaction is written in two places: in the bank column of the cash book, kept by the business, and in the business's account in the bank's own books. The pass book (or the bank statement — loose sheets, a PDF or a net-banking download) is simply a copy of that account as kept by the bank.

The two records look at the same money from opposite ends. For the business, money lying in the bank is an asset — the bank owes it — so the cash book shows a debit balance. For the bank, the same money is a liability owed to its customer, so the pass book shows a credit balance. A credit balance in the pass book is therefore "favourable", and a debit balance in the pass book means an overdraft (the customer owes the bank), which appears as a credit balance in the cash book.

Banks also do many things for customers that later appear in the pass book: collecting cheques, bills, dividends and interest; paying premiums, EMIs and utility bills on standing instructions; discounting bills; granting overdrafts and loans; and charging fees for these services.
concepts.analogy: Two friends keep a note of a loan between them. The lender writes "Ravi owes me ₹500" and Ravi writes "I owe ₹500". Same fact, opposite sides — exactly like the cash book and the pass book.
concepts.work: At year-end every auditor obtains a bank balance confirmation directly from the bank. The first thing checked is whether the balance in the client's books can be reconciled to that confirmation.

concepts.title: What a Bank Reconciliation Statement is — and why it matters
body: A Bank Reconciliation Statement (BRS) is a working statement, prepared by the account holder on a particular date, that starts from the bank balance in one record, lists every cause of difference, and arrives at the balance in the other record. It is not a ledger account and it does not by itself correct anything.

Why bother? (i) It throws up errors made in the cash book or by the bank. (ii) It shows cheques that are taking unusually long to clear. (iii) It is an internal control: a cashier who records deposits in the cash book but pockets the money is caught quickly when someone independent reconciles every month. (iv) It reveals the true bank position after allowing for items still in the pipeline, and makes sure every bank transaction for the period is actually recorded.

Many past corporate frauds involved manipulated bank balances or fake bank statements, which is why reconciliation is now a routine part of internal control. Frequency depends on size and volume — large businesses reconcile daily or weekly, small ones monthly or quarterly.
concepts.analogy: A BRS is like checking your phone's expense app against your bank SMS alerts at the end of the month — any gap is either a delay, something you forgot to note, or a mistake somebody made.
concepts.work: In an audit, an old "cheque deposited but not credited" that never clears is a classic red flag for teeming and lading or a fictitious receipt. Seniors often ask articled assistants to trace every reconciling item to the next month's bank statement.

concepts.title: Why the two balances differ
body: Timing gaps: a transaction is recorded by the business and the bank on different dates. Cheques issued are written in the cash book on the day of issue, but the bank records them only when the payee presents them. Cheques deposited are written in the cash book immediately, but the bank credits them only after collection (clearing).

Transactions the bank records first: interest credited, dividends or interest on investments collected, bills collected, direct deposits by customers through NEFT/RTGS/UPI, bank charges, locker rent, interest on overdraft, payments made under standing instructions (insurance, EMIs), and cheques or discounted bills dishonoured. The business learns of these only when it sees the statement.

Errors: by the business (amount written wrongly, entry made twice or omitted, totals overcast or undercast, entry on the wrong side, a receipt written in the bank column instead of the cash column) or by the bank (crediting or debiting the wrong customer's account).

blocks.title: Add or less? (When you start from an overdraft, every sign flips.)
blocks.note: Shortcut: ask "which record shows MORE money right now because of this item?" If the starting record shows more, deduct; if it shows less, add. A negative final answer means the other record shows an overdraft.

concepts.analogy: A parcel booked today is in your "sent" list at once but appears in the receiver's "received" list only after delivery — the gap is timing, not a mistake.
concepts.work: In accounting software, the "bank reconciliation" screen lets you tick each cash-book entry with its bank date; whatever stays unticked is exactly the list of reconciling items for the BRS.

concepts.title: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points
body: You may start from any of four balances: debit (favourable) balance as per cash book, credit (overdraft) balance as per cash book, credit (favourable) balance as per pass book, or debit (overdraft) balance as per pass book. The answer is the balance in the other record.

Do not memorise a list — reason it out. Take each item and ask: because of this item, does the record I started from show more money or less money than the other record? If it shows more, deduct; if it shows less, add. Example: a cheque issued but not presented has already reduced the cash book but not the bank — the cash book shows less — so starting from the cash book you add it.

When you start from an overdraft, treat the overdraft as a negative balance: every add becomes less and every less becomes add. If you start from a favourable balance and the answer comes out negative, the other record shows an overdraft of that amount (and vice versa).
concepts.analogy: Two thermometers that should read the same: if one reads higher because of a known reason, you subtract that reason from it to get the other reading.
concepts.work: Reviewers in practice check the sign of each reconciling item against this "which shows more?" logic — the most common error in a client-prepared BRS is a sign error on an overdraft account.

concepts.title: Two layouts: "balance" and "plus & minus"
body: Balance presentation: start with the balance, show "Add:" items, a sub-total, then "Less:" items, and end with the balance as per the other record. A negative figure is shown in brackets.

Plus & minus presentation: two amount columns. The starting balance goes in the plus column if favourable and in the minus column if it is an overdraft; each item goes in the plus or minus column; the closing balance is the figure that makes both columns equal. Both columns are then totalled — a built-in arithmetic check.
Whichever layout you use, write a heading with the name and "Bank Reconciliation Statement as on <date>" — a BRS is always as on a date, not for a period.

concepts.analogy: Balance presentation reads like a story; plus & minus is like a scale where both pans must weigh the same.
concepts.work: Audit working papers usually show the BRS in balance form, with each reconciling item cross-referenced to the next month's bank statement where it finally cleared.

concepts.title: Adjusted (amended) cash book method
body: Here the cash book is first corrected for everything that is the business's own omission or error — bank charges, interest, direct deposits and payments, collections, dishonoured cheques or bills, and mistakes in the cash book itself (wrong amounts, double entries, casting errors). The corrected figure is the adjusted cash book balance.

Only the items that remain — timing gaps (cheques issued but not presented, cheques deposited but not cleared) and errors made by the bank — are taken to the BRS, which then starts from the adjusted balance. An item adjusted in the cash book is never repeated in the BRS, and the bank's errors are never put in the cash book.

For a monthly reconciliation the adjusted cash book is optional. At the year-end it should be prepared, because the balance sheet must show the correct bank balance as per the business's books — that is, the adjusted cash book balance, not the pass book balance.
concepts.analogy: Before comparing your notes with a friend's, you first fix your own spelling mistakes; only then do you list the differences that are genuinely "theirs" or "not yet".
concepts.work: At the year-end the accountant passes journal entries for bank charges, interest, direct receipts and dishonoured cheques before finalising accounts — this is the adjusted cash book in practice.

concepts.title: Working from the actual cash book and bank statement
body: In practice you are not handed a list of differences — you must find them. Tick each entry in the cash book against the bank statement (receipts against deposits, payments against withdrawals). Unticked cash-book receipts are deposits not yet credited; unticked cash-book payments are cheques not yet presented; unticked bank-statement entries are items the bank recorded first.
If the BRS is for an earlier date (say 31 March) and you are also given the next month's statement, the March items that appear in April's statement confirm the timing differences as on 31 March.

concepts.work: Bank feeds in modern software auto-match most entries; the accountant's real job is investigating the unmatched few — duplicate payments, missed receipts and charges.

Signs flip for an overdraft
solution.text: An unpresented cheque means the bank has not yet paid it, so the bank's overdraft is smaller — deduct from the overdraft. An uncleared deposit means the bank has not yet reduced the overdraft — add. Interest and the dishonoured cheque increase the bank's overdraft — add. The dividend reduces it — deduct.

jobs.title: Year-end bank audit at a distributor
jobs.role: Articled assistant on a statutory audit
jobs.situation: The client's BRS as on 31 March shows ₹4.6 lakh of "cheques deposited but not credited", including a ₹1.2 lakh cheque dated 12 January. There is also an "unpresented" cheque of ₹80,000 issued in September.
steps: Obtain the bank's balance confirmation directly and agree the pass-book figure in the BRS to it.
Trace each "deposited but not credited" item to the April bank statement. A deposit made in March should clear within a few days; one dated January that is still uncleared is not a timing difference.
Ask for the deposit slip and the customer's ledger for the January cheque — a receipt recorded in the books but never banked can hide misappropriation (teeming and lading).
For the September cheque: a cheque not presented for months may be stale (cheques are generally valid for three months). It may need to be written back to the supplier's account.
Record findings with cross-references and propose adjustments to the senior.
jobs.takeaway: A BRS is only as good as its reconciling items. Every item should clear in the next statement — old items are the auditor's first lead.
jobs.think: Why is a deposit that never clears more dangerous than a cheque that is never presented?
jobs.answer: An uncleared deposit means the books show money that may never have reached the bank — the asset may be fictitious or stolen. An unpresented cheque at worst means a liability is still owed.

jobs.title: Monthly reconciliation with a UPI-heavy bank account
jobs.role: Accounts executive in a retail chain
jobs.situation: Your store account receives hundreds of UPI credits a day. The bank statement for June shows ₹38,400 of credits that nobody has recorded, plus payment-gateway charges of ₹2,150.
steps: Import the bank statement into the accounting software and run auto-matching against the cash book.
For the unmatched credits, download the UPI settlement report and identify the customers or stores.
Pass entries for the gateway charges and the identified receipts — these belong in the adjusted cash book.
Keep genuinely unidentified credits in a suspense account and follow up; do not simply leave them out.
Prepare the BRS showing only timing items and file it with the month-end pack.
jobs.takeaway: Items the bank records first must be brought into the books promptly; otherwise both profit and receivables are misstated.

mcqs.q: A pass book is a copy of:
options: The customer's account in the books of the bank
The bank account in the customer's books
The cash book of the customer
mcqs.explain: A pass book (or bank statement) is prepared by the bank from its own ledger, so it is a copy of the customer's account as it appears in the bank's books. The tempting option, the bank account in the customer's books, describes the bank column of the customer's cash book — the record the pass book is compared with, not the pass book itself. In practice: businesses download bank statements from net banking every month and reconcile them with the bank ledger in Tally.
mcqs.topic: Pass book versus the cash book's bank column

mcqs.q: A credit balance in the pass book indicates:
options: A favourable balance, equal to a debit balance in the cash book
A credit balance in the cash book
mcqs.explain: For the bank, a customer's deposit is money it owes, a liability, so it shows a credit balance in the pass book. For the customer, the same money is an asset, a debit balance in its cash book. So a credit balance in the pass book is favourable and equals a debit balance in the cash book. The tempting option, an overdraft, is the opposite: a debit balance in the pass book. In practice: 'Cr' after the closing balance on a bank statement means money in the account.
mcqs.topic: Pass book versus the cash book's bank column

mcqs.q: Starting with the debit balance as per cash book, cheques issued but not yet presented are:
mcqs.explain: When a cheque is issued, the business credits its bank column at once, but the bank reduces the balance only when the cheque is presented. So the cash book balance is lower than the pass book balance, and the amount is added to reach the pass book figure. The tempting option, deducting, reverses the logic. In practice: at month end, cheques given to suppliers but not yet encashed are the most common reconciling item.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: Starting with the overdraft as per pass book, cheques deposited but not yet credited are:
options: Shown in the adjusted cash book
mcqs.explain: When a cheque is deposited, the business reduces its overdraft in the cash book at once, but the bank does so only after clearing. So the pass book shows a bigger overdraft than the cash book, and the amount is deducted from the pass book overdraft to reach the cash book overdraft. The tempting option, adding, would make the overdraft even bigger. In practice: businesses on cash credit accounts see this daily, because collections deposited late in the day clear only the next working day.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: Cash book debit balance ₹40,000; cheques issued not presented ₹6,000; cheques deposited not credited ₹9,000; bank charges in pass book only ₹500. Balance as per pass book:
mcqs.explain: Starting from the cash book debit balance of ₹40,000: add unpresented cheques ₹6,000 (the bank has not yet paid them), deduct uncleared deposits ₹9,000 (the bank has not yet credited them) and deduct bank charges ₹500 (debited only by the bank). Pass book balance = 40,000 + 6,000 − 9,000 − 500 = ₹36,500. The tempting ₹37,500 forgets the bank charges. In practice: bank charges, SMS fees and GST on them are often first noticed during reconciliation.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: Which of these is taken to the adjusted cash book rather than to the BRS?
options: Bank charges not yet recorded in the cash book
An amount wrongly debited by the bank
mcqs.explain: The adjusted cash book records items that the business itself has not yet entered, such as bank charges shown only in the pass book. Timing differences (unpresented cheques, uncleared deposits) and the bank's own errors are not the business's omissions, so they remain in the BRS. The tempting option, an amount wrongly debited by the bank, is the bank's mistake; it is taken to the BRS and the bank is asked to correct it. In practice: bank charges are booked as an expense once the statement arrives.

mcqs.q: Overdraft as per cash book ₹25,000; cheques issued not presented ₹8,000; interest on overdraft ₹1,200 debited by the bank only. Overdraft as per pass book:
mcqs.explain: Unpresented cheques have already increased the overdraft in the cash book, but not yet at the bank, so the bank's overdraft is smaller: deduct ₹8,000. Interest on overdraft has been debited only by the bank, making its overdraft bigger: add ₹1,200. Pass book overdraft = 25,000 − 8,000 + 1,200 = ₹18,200. The tempting ₹31,800 adds the cheques and deducts the interest. In practice: interest on cash credit is debited monthly by the bank and recorded on reconciliation.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: Starting with the debit balance as per cash book, overcasting of the debit side of the bank column is:
mcqs.explain: Overcasting the debit (receipts) side of the bank column makes the cash book show a higher balance than it should. The bank has no such error, so, starting from the cash book debit balance, the excess is deducted to reach the pass book balance. The tempting option, adding, would widen the gap. In practice: casting errors are rare in computerised books but still appear in manually kept cash books of small businesses.

mcqs.q: The bank balance shown in the balance sheet at the year-end is:
mcqs.explain: The balance sheet shows the correct bank balance as per the business's own books, after recording all omissions (bank charges, direct deposits, dishonours) and correcting its own errors — that is, the adjusted cash book balance. The tempting option, the pass book balance, still differs because of timing items such as unpresented cheques. In practice: auditors check that the bank balance in the balance sheet matches the adjusted ledger and verify it with the BRS and a bank confirmation.

mcqs.q: Starting from the credit balance as per pass book, a cheque deposited and dishonoured (not yet entered in the cash book) is:
mcqs.explain: The cash book still shows the dishonoured cheque as deposited, but the bank has reversed it, so the pass book balance is lower than the cash book balance. Starting from the pass book balance, add the amount to reach the cash book balance. The tempting option, deducting, is the treatment when starting from the cash book side. In practice: dishonoured customer cheques must be recorded quickly, because the customer owes the money again and a cheque bounce may lead to action under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: Pass book credit balance ₹80,000. A customer's direct deposit of ₹12,000 is not yet in the cash book; there is no other difference. Balance as per cash book:
mcqs.explain: The bank has already credited the customer's direct deposit, while the business has yet to record it, so the pass book balance is higher. Starting from the pass book credit balance, deduct: ₹80,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹68,000. The tempting ₹92,000 adds the deposit, which would count it twice. In practice: customers frequently pay through NEFT, RTGS or UPI directly into the business account, and the accountant learns of it only from the statement.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

options: A statement prepared by the account holder as on a date
A ledger account prepared by the bank
Part of the double entry system
Prepared for a period, like a profit and loss account
mcqs.explain: A Bank Reconciliation Statement is prepared by the account holder to explain the difference between the cash book and pass book balances as on a particular date. It is a working statement, outside the double-entry system, so nothing is posted from it. The tempting option, a statement prepared for a period like a profit and loss account, is wrong because a BRS explains balances at one date. In practice: companies prepare BRS monthly, and auditors review them as an internal control check.
mcqs.topic: What a Bank Reconciliation Statement is — and why it matters

mcqs.q: A cheque of ₹4,000 deposited was wrongly entered on the credit side of the bank column. Starting from the debit balance as per cash book, you should:
mcqs.explain: The deposit should have increased the cash book by ₹4,000 but was entered on the credit side, decreasing it by ₹4,000. So the cash book is understated by 2 × ₹4,000 = ₹8,000. Starting from the cash book debit balance, add ₹8,000 to reach the pass book. The tempting ₹4,000 corrects only half the error. In practice: wrong-side entries always create a difference of double the amount, which helps accountants trace them.

questions.q: On 31 December 2026 the pass book of Kapoor Electronics showed a credit balance of ₹2,46,300. Prepare a Bank Reconciliation Statement from the following: (1) cheques issued during December ₹1,10,000, of which only ₹64,000 were presented before 31 December; (2) cheques deposited ₹92,000, of which ₹61,500 were credited by 31 December; (3) a cheque of ₹8,000 received was recorded in the bank column but not sent to the bank; (4) the bank collected a bill receivable of ₹25,000 directly; (5) interest allowed ₹1,900 and bank charges ₹650 appear only in the pass book.

questions.q: What is a Bank Reconciliation Statement? Why may the bank balance in the cash book not agree with the pass book? Give one example for each reason.

model.text: A Bank Reconciliation Statement is a statement prepared by the account holder, as on a given date, that starts from the bank balance in one record (cash book or pass book), lists every reason for the gap and arrives at the balance in the other record.

items: Timing differences — the same transaction is recorded by the two parties on different dates; e.g. a cheque issued on 30 March is in the cash book at once but reaches the bank only when presented on 3 April.

Transactions recorded first by the bank — e.g. bank charges, interest credited, dividends collected, payments under standing instructions or direct deposits by customers, which the business records only after seeing the statement.
Errors by the business — e.g. a receipt entered twice in the bank column, or casting errors.
Errors by the bank — e.g. a cheque of another customer wrongly debited to the account.

viva.q: What is a bank reconciliation statement, and why is it prepared?
viva.model: A bank reconciliation statement is a statement prepared by the account holder on a particular date which starts from the cash book bank balance, lists every cause of difference and arrives at the pass book balance, so the two are reconciled. It is prepared to detect errors and frauds, as an internal control, to find out delays in clearing of cheques, and to know the true bank balance.

viva.q: Why does a credit balance in the pass book mean the same thing as a debit balance in the cash book?
viva.model: Because the two records are kept by opposite parties. The pass book is the bank's copy of the customer's account; for the bank the customer's money is a liability, so it shows a credit balance. In the customer's cash book the bank owes that money, so the bank is like a debtor, an asset, and the balance is a debit.

cases.title: Shinde Motors — year-end reconciliation
cases.case: Shinde Motors closes its books on 31 March 2027. On that date its cash book shows a debit bank balance of ₹2,65,000, while the bank statement shows a credit balance of ₹2,57,500. On checking: (a) a customer paid ₹30,000 directly into the bank — not yet recorded; (b) bank charges ₹1,500 appear only in the statement; (c) a customer's cheque of ₹18,000 deposited in March was dishonoured — not yet recorded; (d) cheques issued ₹52,000 had not been presented; (e) cheques deposited ₹70,000 had not been credited.

mcqs.q: Which items should be passed through the adjusted cash book?
mcqs.explain: The adjusted cash book records items the business has not yet entered: the direct deposit (a), bank charges (b) and the dishonoured cheque (c). Unpresented cheques (d) and uncleared deposits (e) are timing differences — the cash book is already correct, and the bank will catch up — so they stay in the BRS. The tempting option, (a) to (e), would wrongly reverse correct entries. In practice: auditors check that only genuine omissions are adjusted in the books.

mcqs.q: What is the adjusted cash book balance?
mcqs.explain: Adjusted cash book balance = ₹2,65,000 + direct deposit ₹30,000 − bank charges ₹1,500 − dishonoured cheque ₹18,000 = ₹2,75,500. The tempting ₹2,77,000 omits the bank charges. Unpresented cheques and uncleared deposits are not adjusted because the cash book already recorded them correctly. In practice: the accountant passes these three entries in the books and then prepares the BRS from the corrected balance.

mcqs.q: Starting from the adjusted balance, what is the pass book balance as per the BRS?
mcqs.explain: Starting from the adjusted cash book balance of ₹2,75,500: add unpresented cheques ₹52,000 (the bank has not yet paid them) and deduct uncleared deposits ₹70,000 (the bank has not yet credited them). Pass book balance = 2,75,500 + 52,000 − 70,000 = ₹2,57,500, matching the statement. The tempting ₹2,93,500 reverses both items. In practice: once the BRS agrees, any remaining unreconciled difference signals an error to investigate.
mcqs.topic: Add or less — the logic, and the four starting points

mcqs.q: At what figure is the bank balance shown in the balance sheet on 31 March 2027?
mcqs.explain: The balance sheet shows the bank balance as per the corrected books — the adjusted cash book balance of ₹2,75,500 — not the bank statement figure. The tempting ₹2,57,500 is the bank statement balance, which differs only because of timing items (d) and (e) that will clear soon. ₹2,65,000 is wrong because it ignores the omissions. In practice: auditors verify this figure with the BRS and a balance confirmation obtained directly from the bank.
